sections.title: The Three-Part Condition
sections.body:
A limit deliberately ignores the point it is aimed at. The value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ is decided entirely by what $f$ does **near** $a$ and never by $f(a)$ itself - that was the whole purpose of the deleted neighbourhood. **Continuity** is the extra demand that the point and its neighbourhood finally agree.

A function $f$ is **continuous at $a$** when three things hold: $f(a)$ is defined; $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists; and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. Compressed into one sentence, continuity at $a$ says exactly this: *the limit may be computed by substitution*. Every limit you have ever evaluated by plugging the number in was a use of continuity you had not yet been told about.

The three clauses look redundant, and they are not. Each can fail while the other two survive - $(x^2-4)/(x-2)$ has a limit at $2$ and no value there; $|x|/x$ has neither at $0$; a function pinned to a stray value at one point has both and they disagree. No two of the clauses imply the third, which is why the definition is a list rather than a slogan.

Continuity **on an open interval** $(a,b)$ means continuity at every point of it. At the endpoint of a closed interval $[a,b]$ only one side of the point exists, so we ask only for $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)$ - **one-sided continuity**. Without that concession $\sqrt{x}$ would count as discontinuous at $0$ merely because the left half of the picture is not there to be checked.
sections.code:
CONTINUOUS AT a  requires all three, and in this order:

   (1)  f(a) is defined         the point is there at all
   (2)  lim f(x)  exists        the neighbourhood agrees with itself
        x->a
   (3)  lim f(x) = f(a)         point and neighbourhood agree
        x->a

Each one can fail while the other two survive:

   f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2)            at a = 2
        f(2) = 0/0 is UNDEFINED           -> (1) fails
        the limit is 4, so (2) is fine

   f(x) = |x| / x                      at a = 0
        one-sided limits are -1 and +1    -> (2) fails
        there is no single limit for anything to be compared with

   f(x) = { x^2   for x =/= 1
          {  5    for x  =  1          at a = 1
        f(1) = 5 exists, the limit is 1, and 5 =/= 1
        -> (3) fails: both halves exist and simply disagree

AT AN ENDPOINT ONLY ONE SIDE EXISTS

   sqrt(x) on [0, oo):     lim   sqrt(x) = 0 = sqrt(0)
                          x->0+

   so sqrt is continuous FROM THE RIGHT at 0, and that is all we ask of
   an endpoint. Otherwise no function on a closed interval could ever be
   called continuous, and the theorems that need [a, b] would be empty.

annotations.text: Clause (3) is the one that does the work: it is what licenses substitution. Clauses (1) and (2) exist only so that (3) has two sides to compare.
A two-sided limit exists only when both sides agree. Here they disagree by a fixed amount, so no repair at the single point x = 0 can help.
This is the case people forget exists. The function is defined, the limit exists, and it is still discontinuous - because nobody made them equal.
One-sided continuity at an endpoint is a genuine weakening of the definition, adopted because the alternative is useless, not because it is a technicality.

checkpoint.prompt: Take $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ at $a = 2$. Fill each blank exactly as instructed.
checkpoint.template:
f(2) is ___                       (write defined or undefined)
the limit as x -> 2 is ___         (a number)
the first condition to fail is number ___
checkpoint.explain: Substituting $2$ gives $0/0$, so $f(2)$ does not exist and clause $(1)$ fails immediately. The limit is unaffected: cancelling the common factor leaves $x+2 \to 4$, because a limit never asks about $x = 2$ itself. The tempting answer for the second blank is *does not exist* - but a missing value and a missing limit are different failures, and confusing them is the commonest error on this floor.

sections.title: Three Ways the Condition Fails
sections.body:
A discontinuity is not one phenomenon, and the classification is far more useful than the bare word. A **removable** discontinuity is one where $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ exists but $f(a)$ is missing or is some other number: the graph has a **hole**, and defining $f(a) = L$ repairs it in one stroke.

A **jump** discontinuity has both one-sided limits finite but different. Nothing repairs it, because whatever value you assign to $f(a)$ disagrees with at least one side - and altering a function at a single point never moves a limit anyway. The size of the jump, $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f - \lim_{x \to a^-} f$, is a genuine measurement, which is why step functions and tax bands live here.

An **infinite** discontinuity has at least one one-sided limit equal to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$, and the line $x = a$ is then a **vertical asymptote**. Since $\infty$ is not a value, this is really clause $(2)$ failing - the limit does not exist - dressed in more informative language.

For a rational function the whole classification is settled by factoring. A denominator zero whose factor **cancels** leaves a hole; one that **survives** leaves an asymptote. A zero denominator on its own tells you which points to examine and nothing whatever about which species you have found.
sections.code:
f(x) = (x^2 - x - 6)/(x^2 - 9)  =  ((x - 3)(x + 2)) / ((x - 3)(x + 3))

Two bad points, and they are NOT the same kind of bad.

  x = 3     the factor (x - 3) cancels
            lim  f(x) = lim (x + 2)/(x + 3) = 5/6      finite
            x->3
            f(3) is undefined       ->  REMOVABLE
            patch it: define f(3) = 5/6 and f is continuous there

  x = -3    the factor (x + 3) does NOT cancel
            numerator -> 6, denominator -> 0
            lim   f(x) = +oo        lim   f(x) = -oo
            x->-3-                  x->-3+
            ->  INFINITE, a vertical asymptote at x = -3
            no value assigned to f(-3) can ever repair this

THE THIRD SPECIES IS A JUMP

  f(x) = { 2x + 1   for x <  1
         { x^2 + 3  for x >= 1

            left limit = 3      right limit = 4      both finite
            3 =/= 4   ->  JUMP, of size 1
            f(1) = 4, so f is continuous from the right at 1 and is
            nowhere near continuous from the left

THE TEST IS THE CANCELLING, NOT THE ZERO DENOMINATOR

  a factor that cancels  -> hole      (removable)
  a factor that survives -> asymptote (infinite)

Three species is not a complete list for every function - sin(1/x) at
x = 0 oscillates too fast to be any of them - but it is complete for
every rational and piecewise function on this floor.

annotations.text: Removable does not mean harmless - f really is discontinuous at 3 as written. It means one edit at one point fixes it, which is untrue of the other two species.
The two sides run to opposite infinities because (x + 3) changes sign at -3 while the numerator does not. Odd-order surviving factors flip; even-order ones do not.
Both one-sided limits exist and are finite. That is exactly what separates a jump from an infinite discontinuity, and it is the only thing that does.
Read this line before answering any classification question. Anyone who hunts only for zeros of the denominator calls every one of them an asymptote, and is wrong about half of them.

checkpoint.prompt: Classify each discontinuity. Give the first answer as a number, and each of the others as one of `removable`, `jump` or `infinite`.

steps.label: kind of discontinuity of (x^3 - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1
kind of discontinuity of 1/(x - 1)^2 at x = 1
kind of discontinuity of |x|/x at x = 0

checkpoint.explain: $x^3 - 1 = (x-1)(x^2+x+1)$, so the offending factor cancels and the limit is $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$: a hole, repaired by setting $f(1) = 3$. In $1/(x-1)^2$ nothing cancels and the limit is $+\infty$ from both sides - an even power, so no sign flip. And $|x|/x$ is $-1$ left of $0$ and $+1$ right of it: two finite disagreeing limits, a jump of size $2$, and not - despite the fraction - anything infinite.

sections.title: Built Continuous, Then Trusted
sections.body:
Almost nothing is proved continuous from the definition twice. Constants and $x$ are continuous; sums, products and quotients of continuous functions are continuous wherever the denominator is non-zero; and a composition $f(g(x))$ is continuous at $a$ whenever $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(a)$. Everything else is assembled from those.

Two consequences carry most of the weight. **Every polynomial is continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}$**, and **every rational function is continuous exactly on its domain** - so the only candidate discontinuities of $p(x)/q(x)$ sit at zeros of $q$, and nowhere else at all. Composition extends the same convenience to $\sqrt{x^2-4}$ or $\cos(x^3)$, where the trouble is located by inspecting the inside function.

This matters because continuity is the hypothesis of the first genuinely powerful theorem in the subject. The **Intermediate Value Theorem** says that if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $N$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c) = N$ for at least one $c$ in $(a,b)$: a continuous function cannot get from one value to another without passing through everything in between.

The honest use is **root bracketing**. Take $N = 0$, so that opposite signs at the endpoints guarantee a root inside; then halve the interval while preserving the sign change and the root is located to any accuracy you like. What the theorem never supplies is uniqueness, a formula, or a position - and it collapses entirely if continuity fails anywhere in $[a,b]$, which is how $1/x$ manages to run from $-1$ to $1$ on $[-1,1]$ without ever being zero.
sections.code:
BUILDING BLOCKS

  constants and x            continuous on all of R
  sums and products          continuous wherever the pieces are
  quotients                  continuous wherever the denominator =/= 0
  compositions               f(g(x)) is continuous at a whenever g is
                             continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a)

  => every polynomial is continuous on (-oo, oo)
  => every rational function is continuous exactly on its own domain
  => sqrt(x^2 - 4) is continuous on (-oo, -2] and on [2, oo)

INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM

  f continuous on the CLOSED interval [a, b], and N lying between
  f(a) and f(b)
    ==>  there is at least one c in (a, b) with f(c) = N.

ROOT BRACKETING is the case N = 0: a SIGN CHANGE guarantees a root.

  g(x) = x^3 - x - 1  is a polynomial, hence continuous on [1, 2]

     g(1) = -1 < 0        g(2) = 5 > 0        sign change
     ==> a root exists somewhere in (1, 2)

  Halve the bracket, keeping whichever half still changes sign:

     g(3/2)  =    7/8  > 0   ->  root in (1, 3/2)
     g(5/4)  = -19/64  < 0   ->  root in (5/4, 3/2)
     g(11/8) = 115/512 > 0   ->  root in (5/4, 11/8)

  The true root is 1.3247179...; three halvings have pinned it inside a
  bracket of width 1/8 without solving a cubic at all.

WHAT THE THEOREM DOES NOT SAY

  not unique     f may hit the value N many times over
  not located    it names no c, only an interval that contains one
  not optional   on [-1, 1], f(x) = 1/x runs from -1 up to 1 and is
                 never 0 - it is discontinuous at 0, so the theorem
                 was never available in the first place

annotations.text: This one line saves most of the work on the floor: to find a rational function's discontinuities, factor the denominator and look nowhere else.
Closed, and continuous at every point of it. One bad point anywhere inside voids the conclusion outright rather than merely weakening it.
The sign change is the entire input. The size of the values is irrelevant: -0.001 and +0.001 would prove precisely as much.
IVT is an existence theorem and nothing more. Reading it as 'there is exactly one root' is the standard overclaim, and x^3 - x has three roots in [-2, 2] to disprove it.

checkpoint.prompt: Let $p(x) = x^3 - 4x + 1$. Show that $p$ has a root in $(0,1)$, naming the hypothesis of the Intermediate Value Theorem you rely on, then perform one bisection step to halve the bracket. State what you have and have not established about the number of roots.
checkpoint.answer: p is a polynomial, so it is continuous on the closed interval [0, 1]. p(0) = 1 > 0 and p(1) = 1 - 4 + 1 = -2 < 0, so 0 lies between p(0) and p(1) and the Intermediate Value Theorem supplies a c in (0,1) with p(c) = 0. Bisecting: p(1/2) = 1/8 - 2 + 1 = -7/8 < 0, so the sign change now sits between 0 and 1/2 and the root lies in (0, 1/2). This establishes that at least one root exists there; it establishes nothing about uniqueness, and indeed p(2) = 1 > 0, so a second root lies in (1, 2).
checkpoint.explain: $p(0) = 1$ and $p(1) = -2$ have opposite signs, and $p$ is a polynomial so continuity on $[0,1]$ comes for free - that is the hypothesis, and it is the only one. The midpoint value $p(1/2) = -7/8$ is negative, so the sign change now lies between $0$ and $1/2$ and the bracket halves to $(0, 1/2)$. The overclaim to avoid is *therefore the root is unique*: $p(2) = 1$ is positive again, so there is a second root in $(1,2)$ that this argument knew nothing about.

sections.title: Behaviour at the Ends
sections.body:
$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L$ means $f(x)$ can be forced as close to $L$ as you please by taking $x$ large enough. Nothing about it is a limit *at a point*: $\infty$ is a direction rather than a place, there is no $f(\infty)$, and the three-part condition has nothing to say. When such a limit exists, the line $y = L$ is a **horizontal asymptote** of the graph.

One fact drives every computation: $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x^k} = 0$ for every $k > 0$. Dividing the numerator and denominator of a rational function by the highest power appearing in the **denominator** turns every remaining term into some $1/x^k$, and the answer falls out.

That yields a trichotomy worth memorising. If $\deg p < \deg q$ then $p/q \to 0$; if $\deg p = \deg q$ the limit is the ratio of the **leading coefficients**; if $\deg p > \deg q$ the quotient runs off to $\pm\infty$ and there is no horizontal asymptote at all. The constant terms never matter - end behaviour is decided by the largest powers alone.

Two warnings. Square roots flip sign: $\sqrt{x^2} = |x| = -x$ when $x < 0$, so $\sqrt{4x^2+1}/(3x-5) \to 2/3$ as $x \to \infty$ but $\to -2/3$ as $x \to -\infty$, giving **two** horizontal asymptotes rather than one. And a graph may cross its horizontal asymptote as often as it likes, because the definition constrains the tail and never the middle.
sections.code:
lim   f(x) = L   means f(x) can be forced as close to L as you like by
x->oo            taking x large enough. "oo" is a DIRECTION, not a place,
                 so there is no f(oo) to compare anything with and no
                 three-part condition to check here.

                 y = L is then a HORIZONTAL ASYMPTOTE of the graph.

EVERYTHING RESTS ON ONE FACT:     lim  1/x^k = 0    for every k > 0
                                 x->oo

RATIONAL FUNCTIONS: divide top and bottom by the largest power below.

  (3x^2 - 5x + 1)/(2x^2 + 7)     divide through by x^2
      = (3 - 5/x + 1/x^2)/(2 + 7/x^2)  ->  3/2      HA:  y = 3/2

  (2x + 1)/(x^2 - 3)             bottom wins   ->  0      HA:  y = 0

  (x^3 + 1)/(4x^2 - x)           top wins      ->  +oo    NO horizontal
                                                          asymptote

  degree top  <  degree bottom   ->  y = 0
  degree top  =  degree bottom   ->  y = (leading top)/(leading bottom)
  degree top  >  degree bottom   ->  no horizontal asymptote at all

ROOTS FLIP SIGNS:   sqrt(x^2) = |x|,   which is -x when x < 0.

  sqrt(4x^2 + 1)/(3x - 5)   ->   2/3   as x -> +oo
                            ->  -2/3   as x -> -oo

Two horizontal asymptotes, and the minus sign is not a slip: a square
root is never negative, so for very negative x the top stays positive
while the bottom has gone negative.

A graph is also perfectly free to CROSS its horizontal asymptote - the
definition constrains the tail, not the middle.

annotations.text: This is why 'continuous at infinity' is a meaningless phrase. A limit at infinity describes a tail; continuity describes a point.
Below, meaning in the denominator. Dividing by the largest power found anywhere is the usual slip, and it turns a finite answer into 0 or into an unresolved infinity.
No horizontal asymptote does not mean no end behaviour. When the top wins by exactly one degree there is a slant asymptote instead, which later floors will use.
Whenever a square root of an even power appears, test one large negative number such as x = -1000. It costs ten seconds and catches the commonest error in the section.

checkpoint.prompt: Evaluate each limit as $x \to \infty$, then count asymptotes. Write fractions like `2/3`, and whole numbers as whole numbers.
checkpoint.template:
lim (7x^2 + 3)/(2 - x^2)   = ___
lim (x^2 + 1)/(x^3 - 2)    = ___
number of horizontal asymptotes of (5x - 2)/sqrt(9x^2 + 4): ___
checkpoint.explain: Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients, $7/(-1) = -7$; the leading coefficient of $2 - x^2$ is $-1$, and reading it as $2$ is what produces the wrong answer $7/2$. In the second the denominator wins outright, so the limit is $0$. The third has $\sqrt{9x^2+4} = |x|\sqrt{9 + 4/x^2}$, giving $5/3$ as $x \to \infty$ and $-5/3$ as $x \to -\infty$: two distinct horizontal asymptotes.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$. Answer for the point $a = 3$, writing `defined` or `undefined`, then a number, then one of `removable`, `jump`, `infinite`.
guided-practice.template:
g(3) is ___
the limit as x -> 3 is ___
the discontinuity at x = 3 is ___
the value that would repair it is ___
guided-practice.hint: Factor the numerator as $(x-3)(x+3)$ before doing anything else.
guided-practice.explain: $g(3)$ is $0/0$, so clause $(1)$ fails and $g$ is genuinely discontinuous there. But the factor $(x-3)$ cancels, leaving $x + 3 \to 6$, so the limit exists and the hole can be filled by declaring $g(3) = 6$. The tempting wrong answer is *infinite*, on the grounds that the denominator hits zero; a zero denominator only tells you where to look, and the cancelling tells you what you have found.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the classification procedure for a discontinuity of $f$ at $x = a$ into working order.
fragments: Compute the two one-sided limits of f as x -> a- and as x -> a+.
If either one-sided limit is infinite, stop: the discontinuity is infinite and x = a is a vertical asymptote.
Otherwise both one-sided limits are finite; if they differ, stop: the discontinuity is a jump, of size equal to their difference.
Otherwise they agree, so the two-sided limit L exists; now look at the value f(a).
If f(a) is undefined or differs from L, the discontinuity is removable, and redefining f(a) = L repairs it.
guided-practice.explain: The one-sided limits come first because every later question is asked about them - which species you have depends on whether they are infinite, whether they differ, and only lastly on $f(a)$. Checking $f(a)$ early is the natural instinct and it is wasted work: the value is irrelevant unless the two sides have already agreed on a finite $L$.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 - 3x + 2}$. Factor it, classify the behaviour at every point where the denominator vanishes, give the intervals on which $f$ is continuous, and state its horizontal asymptote.
guided-practice.answer: Factoring gives f(x) = (x-1)(x+1) / ((x-1)(x-2)) = (x+1)/(x-2) for x =/= 1. At x = 1 the factor cancels, so the limit is (1+1)/(1-2) = -2 and the discontinuity is removable; defining f(1) = -2 repairs it. At x = 2 the factor (x-2) survives and the numerator tends to 3, so the limits are -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right: an infinite discontinuity with a vertical asymptote x = 2. As a quotient of polynomials, f is continuous exactly on its domain, namely (-infinity, 1), (1, 2) and (2, infinity). Numerator and denominator both have degree 2 with leading coefficients 1 and 1, so the horizontal asymptote is y = 1.
guided-practice.hint: $x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x-1)(x-2)$. One of those factors meets a matching factor upstairs and one does not.
guided-practice.explain: Both denominator zeros look identical until you factor: $(x-1)$ cancels and $(x-2)$ does not, so $x = 1$ is a hole at height $-2$ while $x = 2$ is a vertical asymptote. Note the hole sits at $y = -2$, not at $y = 0$ - a removable discontinuity has a perfectly ordinary height, and reporting the hole as being 'at zero' is a frequent slip. The horizontal asymptote is $y = 1$ from equal degrees, and it is genuinely unrelated to the vertical one.

guided-practice.prompt: Find the value of $c$ making $$f(x) = \begin{cases} cx + 2 & x < 3 \\ x^2 - c & x \ge 3 \end{cases}$$ continuous at $x = 3$. Set out the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value $f(3)$, and say which of the three clauses of continuity each equality enforces.
guided-practice.answer: The left-hand limit is lim as x -> 3- of (cx + 2) = 3c + 2, since cx + 2 is a polynomial and hence continuous. The right-hand limit is lim as x -> 3+ of (x^2 - c) = 9 - c, and f(3) = 9 - c as well because the second piece is the one that owns x = 3. Clause (1) holds automatically. Clause (2), existence of the two-sided limit, requires the left and right limits to be equal: 3c + 2 = 9 - c, so 4c = 7 and c = 7/4. Clause (3) is then free, since the common limit 3(7/4) + 2 = 29/4 already equals f(3) = 9 - 7/4 = 29/4. So c = 7/4.
guided-practice.hint: Each piece is a polynomial, so each one-sided limit is found by substituting $x = 3$ into that piece.
guided-practice.explain: Each branch is a polynomial, so its one-sided limit is just substitution: $3c+2$ from the left, $9-c$ from the right. Continuity forces $3c + 2 = 9 - c$, hence $c = 7/4$ and a common value of $29/4$. The famous wrong move is to equate the two formulas at some other point, or to solve only $f(3) = $ the left limit while forgetting that $f(3)$ comes from the branch containing $x = 3$; here the $\ge$ decides that the right-hand branch owns the point.

guided-practice.prompt: Evaluate each limit as $x \to \infty$. Write fractions as `3/2`, whole numbers plainly, and for the last row write `none` if there is no horizontal asymptote.
guided-practice.hint: Compare the degrees first; only when they are equal do the coefficients matter.
guided-practice.explain: Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients: $3/2$ in the first, and $-1/3$ in the third, where the numerator's leading coefficient is $-1$ and the visible $1$ is a decoy. In the second the denominator outranks the numerator, so the quotient is squeezed to $0$. In the fourth the numerator wins and the quotient runs to $+\infty$, so there is no horizontal asymptote - answering $\infty$ names the limit but not an asymptote, since a horizontal asymptote must be a real number $L$.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Let $h(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x^2 + 2x - 3}$. Classify the behaviour at both zeros of the denominator, give the exact intervals of continuity, and find the horizontal asymptote. Explain why the horizontal asymptote is **not** the ratio of the leading coefficients here.
continuity-workshop.answer: x^2 + 2x - 3 = (x + 3)(x - 1), so h(x) = 1/(x - 1) for x =/= -3. At x = -3 the factor cancels: the limit is 1/(-3 - 1) = -1/4, so the discontinuity is removable and defining h(-3) = -1/4 repairs it. At x = 1 nothing cancels, the numerator tends to 4, and the one-sided limits are -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right: an infinite discontinuity with the vertical asymptote x = 1. As a rational function h is continuous exactly on its domain: (-infinity, -3), (-3, 1) and (1, infinity). The horizontal asymptote is y = 0, because the degree of the numerator, 1, is strictly less than the degree of the denominator, 2. The ratio-of-leading-coefficients rule applies only when the degrees are equal, so it has no bearing here.
continuity-workshop.hint: Factor the denominator first. Then compare degrees on the **original** expression before quoting any asymptote rule.
continuity-workshop.explain: The numerator $x+3$ is one of the denominator's factors, so $x = -3$ is a hole at height $-1/4$ while $x = 1$ is a vertical asymptote. The intervals of continuity omit both points, because a removable discontinuity is still a discontinuity until somebody actually redefines the function. The horizontal asymptote is $y = 0$ by degree comparison; quoting $1/1$ from the surviving form $1/(x-1)$, or $1/1$ from the visible leading coefficients, both produce the wrong answer $y = 1$.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Let $q(x) = x^5 + x - 1$. Bracket a root of $q$ in $[0,1]$ using the Intermediate Value Theorem, then bisect twice, showing the exact value of $q$ at each midpoint and the surviving bracket after each step.
continuity-workshop.answer: q is a polynomial and so is continuous on the closed interval [0, 1]. q(0) = -1 < 0 and q(1) = 1 > 0, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem with N = 0 there is a c in (0, 1) with q(c) = 0. First bisection: q(1/2) = 1/32 + 1/2 - 1 = -15/32 < 0, matching the sign at 0, so the sign change now lies between 1/2 and 1 and the bracket is (1/2, 1). Second bisection: q(3/4) = 243/1024 + 3/4 - 1 = -13/1024 < 0, so the bracket is (3/4, 1), of width 1/4. The true root is about 0.7549.
continuity-workshop.explain: Continuity is free because $q$ is a polynomial, and the opposite signs $q(0) = -1$, $q(1) = 1$ are the entire hypothesis. The instructive step is the second: $q(3/4) = -13/1024 \approx -0.0127$ is negative but only just, and a calculation rounded to two decimal places would report $0.00$ and destroy the bracket. Sign, not size, is what root bracketing consumes, so it must be determined exactly.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Prove that the equation $\cos x = x$ has a solution in the interval $(0,1)$. Construct a suitable function, justify its continuity from the continuity of its parts, apply the Intermediate Value Theorem explicitly, and state what your argument does not prove.
continuity-workshop.hint: Move everything to one side: let $h(x) = \cos x - x$ and hunt for a zero of $h$.
continuity-workshop.explain: Set $h(x) = \cos x - x$, continuous on $[0,1]$ as a difference of two continuous functions - this is exactly where the algebra of continuity earns its keep, since $h$ is not a polynomial and proving it continuous from the definition would be miserable. Then $h(0) = 1 > 0$ and $h(1) = \cos 1 - 1 \approx -0.4597 < 0$, so the Intermediate Value Theorem with $N = 0$ gives $c \in (0,1)$ with $h(c) = 0$, that is $\cos c = c$. What the argument does not prove is uniqueness, or where $c$ is; the true value is about $0.7391$, and the theorem supplied none of those digits.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Two students misuse the Intermediate Value Theorem. The first argues that since $f(x) = 1/x$ satisfies $f(-1) = -1$ and $f(1) = 1$, it must equal $0$ somewhere in $(-1,1)$. The second argues that since $\tan(\pi/4) = 1$ and $\tan(3\pi/4) = -1$, $\tan x$ must be zero somewhere in $(\pi/4, 3\pi/4)$. Explain precisely which hypothesis each has skipped and what actually happens on those intervals.
continuity-workshop.explain: Both have used the conclusion of a theorem whose hypothesis they never checked: continuity on the **whole closed interval**. $1/x$ has an infinite discontinuity at $0$, which sits inside $(-1,1)$, and it leaps from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ there without passing through any value at all; $\tan x$ has an infinite discontinuity at $\pi/2$, inside $(\pi/4, 3\pi/4)$, and is never zero on that interval. Sign changes are evidence of a root only for continuous functions - for everything else a sign change is just as easily the signature of a vertical asymptote.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Find every horizontal asymptote of $u(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{4x^2 + 1}}{3x - 5}$ and of $v(x) = \dfrac{5x - 2}{\sqrt{9x^2 + 4}}$, taking both $x \to \infty$ and $x \to -\infty$. Explain, using $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$, why each function has two asymptotes rather than one.
continuity-workshop.answer: Write sqrt(4x^2 + 1) = |x| sqrt(4 + 1/x^2). As x -> +infinity, |x| = x, so u(x) -> x*2/(3x) = 2/3. As x -> -infinity, |x| = -x, so u(x) -> -2x/(3x) = -2/3. Hence u has horizontal asymptotes y = 2/3 and y = -2/3. Likewise sqrt(9x^2 + 4) = |x| sqrt(9 + 4/x^2), so v(x) -> 5x/(3x) = 5/3 as x -> +infinity and v(x) -> 5x/(-3x) = -5/3 as x -> -infinity, giving asymptotes y = 5/3 and y = -5/3. Two asymptotes appear because a square root is never negative while the linear part changes sign, so the quotient changes sign between the two ends.
continuity-workshop.hint: Pull $|x|$ out of the square root, then replace $|x|$ by $x$ or by $-x$ according to the direction you are travelling.
continuity-workshop.explain: $\sqrt{4x^2+1} = |x|\sqrt{4 + 1/x^2}$ behaves like $2|x|$, which is $2x$ on the right and $-2x$ on the left - so $u \to 2/3$ and $-2/3$, and $v \to 5/3$ and $-5/3$. The famous wrong answer is a single asymptote $y = 2/3$, produced by writing $\sqrt{4x^2} = 2x$ and forgetting the modulus. Degree counting alone cannot detect this, because degrees carry no sign information.

exam.prompt: By definition, $f$ is continuous at $a$ exactly when:
choices: $f(a)$ is defined and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists
$f(a)$ is defined, $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, and the two are equal
$f$ is defined on some open interval containing $a$
exam.explain: All three clauses are needed, and the third is not implied by the first two: $f(x) = x^2$ for $x \neq 1$ with $f(1) = 5$ satisfies both of the others and is plainly discontinuous. Option $(1)$ describes a removable discontinuity just as happily as a continuous point, and option $(4)$ is a statement about the domain that says nothing about limits at all.

exam.prompt: By definition, the line $y = L$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f$ exactly when:
choices: the numerator and denominator of $f$ have the same degree
exam.explain: A horizontal asymptote is nothing but a finite limit in one of the two directions, and either direction suffices - which is why a function can have two of them. Option $(1)$ is the widespread belief that a graph may not touch its asymptote, and $\sin(x)/x$ crosses $y = 0$ infinitely often to refute it. Option $(3)$ describes a vertical asymptote, and option $(4)$ is a computational rule for one family of functions, not a definition.

exam.prompt: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} & x \neq 2 \\ 7 & x = 2. \end{cases}$$ Give a number, then a clause number, then `removable`, `jump` or `infinite`, then a number.
exam.template:
the limit as x -> 2 is ___
the clause of continuity that fails is number ___
the discontinuity at x = 2 is ___
the single value of f(2) that repairs it is ___
exam.explain: Here $f(2) = 7$ exists and the limit is $4$, so clauses $(1)$ and $(2)$ both hold and only $(3)$ fails - the case that gets forgotten, because nothing is undefined and nothing blows up. It is removable, and the repair is $f(2) = 4$: you move the value to the limit, never the limit to the value, since redefining a function at one point cannot change any limit.

exam.prompt: Evaluate the end behaviour. Write fractions like `2/3` and whole numbers plainly; the last line wants two numbers.
exam.template:
(4x^3 - 2x)/(6x^3 + 5)    -> ___   as x -> oo
(x^2 + 1)/(x^3 - 2)       -> ___   as x -> oo
(6x^4 - x)/(2x^4 + 3x^2)  -> ___   as x -> oo
horizontal asymptotes of 3x/sqrt(x^2 + 1):  y = ___ and y = ___
exam.explain: The first and third have equal degrees, so the answers are $4/6 = 2/3$ and $6/2 = 3$ - lower-order terms are irrelevant however large their coefficients look. The second has a bigger denominator, so the limit is $0$. The last needs $\sqrt{x^2+1} = |x|\sqrt{1 + 1/x^2}$, giving $+3$ to the right and $-3$ to the left; answering with a single asymptote $y = 3$ is the standard casualty of writing $\sqrt{x^2} = x$.

exam.prompt: Order the steps of locating a root by the Intermediate Value Theorem and bisection.
fragments: Check that f is continuous on the whole closed interval [a, b] - a polynomial qualifies outright, a rational one only if no zero of its denominator lies inside.
Evaluate f(a) and f(b) and confirm that they have opposite signs.
Conclude from the Intermediate Value Theorem that f has at least one root in (a, b).
Evaluate f exactly at the midpoint m = (a + b)/2.
Keep whichever half still shows a sign change, and repeat to halve the uncertainty again.
exam.explain: Continuity is checked first because everything after it is invalid without it - a sign change across a vertical asymptote proves nothing whatever. The existence conclusion is drawn before any bisection, since bisection only narrows a root already known to be there; running the halvings on a function with a discontinuity converges perfectly happily onto the asymptote instead.

exam.prompt: Bracket a root of $g(x) = x^3 - x - 1$ on $[1,2]$. Write `negative` or `positive` for the signs, and write brackets exactly in the form `(1, 3/2)`.

steps.label: bracket after then testing the midpoint 5/4

exam.explain: $g(1) = -1$ and $g(2) = 5$, so the sign changes and a root exists in $(1,2)$. Since $g(3/2) = 7/8 > 0$, the sign change is now between $1$ and $3/2$, and you keep the half whose endpoints still disagree - keeping the half containing the larger value is the usual reflex and is exactly backwards. Then $g(5/4) = -19/64 < 0$ narrows it to $(5/4, 3/2)$, which contains the true root $1.3247\ldots$

exam.prompt: Find the value of $b$ making $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + bx & x \le 2 \\ 3x + b & x > 2 \end{cases}$$ continuous at $x = 2$. Give the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and $f(2)$, and say why matching only the two formulas is enough here.
exam.answer: Both branches are polynomials, so each one-sided limit is a substitution. The left-hand limit is 4 + 2b, and since x = 2 belongs to the first branch, f(2) = 4 + 2b as well. The right-hand limit is 6 + b. Continuity requires 4 + 2b = 6 + b, so b = 2, and the common value is 4 + 4 = 8 = 6 + 2. Matching the two formulas suffices because f(2) is produced by one of those same formulas, so once the one-sided limits agree, clause (3) is satisfied automatically.
exam.hint: The $\le$ tells you which branch owns the point $x = 2$, and therefore which formula gives $f(2)$.
exam.explain: Substituting into each branch gives $4 + 2b$ on the left and $6 + b$ on the right, so $b = 2$ and both sides equal $8$. Clause $(3)$ needs no separate work only because $x = 2$ belongs to a branch that is itself continuous there - if the piecewise definition had assigned $f(2)$ some third value, matching the limits would have fixed clause $(2)$ and left a removable discontinuity behind.

exam.prompt: Give every interval on which $H(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x - 1}}{x - 4}$ is continuous, justifying each piece from the continuity rules for compositions and quotients. Say what happens at $x = 1$, what happens at $x = 4$, and why those two points fail for different reasons.
exam.answer: The numerator is the composition of the continuous square root with the polynomial x - 1, so it is defined and continuous wherever x - 1 >= 0, that is on [1, infinity). The denominator is a polynomial, continuous everywhere, and it vanishes only at x = 4. A quotient of continuous functions is continuous wherever the denominator is non-zero, so H is continuous on [1, 4) and on (4, infinity). At x = 1, H is continuous from the right only, because H is not defined at all for x < 1 - there is nothing to the left to check, so this is an endpoint, not a discontinuity. At x = 4 the numerator tends to sqrt(3) =/= 0 while the denominator tends to 0, so the limits are -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right: an infinite discontinuity with the vertical asymptote x = 4.
exam.hint: Two separate constraints: the square root needs $x \ge 1$, and the quotient needs $x \neq 4$.
exam.explain: The rules do all the work: composition gives continuity of $\sqrt{x-1}$ on $[1,\infty)$, and the quotient rule removes only $x = 4$, leaving $[1,4)$ and $(4,\infty)$. The distinction worth internalising is that $x = 1$ is an **endpoint** with one-sided continuity, not a discontinuity - a function cannot be discontinuous where it is not defined on either side - whereas $x = 4$ is a genuine infinite discontinuity sitting inside the domain's reach. Writing the answer as $(1,4) \cup (4,\infty)$ needlessly throws away the point $x = 1$, where $H(1) = 0/(-3) = 0$ is perfectly well behaved.

exam.prompt: Explain why the word *removable* is honest for one species of discontinuity, and why no redefinition of $f$ at a single point can ever remove a jump discontinuity. Use the fact that changing a function at one point changes none of its limits.
exam.explain: At a removable discontinuity the two sides already agree on a single finite $L$, so the only thing wrong is the value at the one point; setting $f(a) = L$ satisfies all three clauses at once. At a jump the two one-sided limits are different numbers, and altering $f$ at $a$ alone leaves both of them exactly as they were - limits are decided by the deleted neighbourhood, never by the point. Whatever value you nominate therefore disagrees with at least one side, so clause $(2)$ stays broken and no repair exists.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{7x^2 + 3}{2 - x^2}$, $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^2 + 1}{x^3 - 2}$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^3 + 1}{4x^2 - x}$. Then state every horizontal asymptote of each of the three functions, writing `none` where there is none, and justify each answer by degrees rather than by inspection.
exam.answer: First: numerator and denominator both have degree 2, so the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients, 7/(-1) = -7. The same holds as x -> -infinity, so y = -7 is the only horizontal asymptote. Second: degree 2 is less than degree 3, so dividing by x^3 gives (1/x + 1/x^3)/(1 - 2/x^3) -> 0. The same holds in the other direction, so y = 0 is the only horizontal asymptote. Third: degree 3 exceeds degree 2, so the quotient behaves like x/4 and tends to +infinity as x -> +infinity, and to -infinity as x -> -infinity. There is no horizontal asymptote at all: none.
exam.hint: Divide through by the highest power in the denominator each time, and read the leading coefficient of $2 - x^2$ carefully.
exam.explain: The answers are $-7$, $0$ and $+\infty$. The first is the classic trap: the leading coefficient of $2 - x^2$ is $-1$, not $2$, so the answer is $7/(-1) = -7$ and not $7/2$ - the constant term is irrelevant however prominently it is written. The third has no horizontal asymptote, because $\infty$ is not a number and an asymptote $y = L$ needs a real $L$; there is a slant asymptote instead, since the numerator wins by exactly one degree.
